question.text: What gap do you need to turn into a flow of traffic?

answer.text: Turning into a flow of traffic needs a gap long enough to finish the turn and reach the speed of the traffic you are joining without disrupting it.

teaching.text: Turn into traffic only with a gap long enough to finish and match the traffic's speed. Remember: room to turn and match.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turning into a flow of traffic needs a gap long enough to finish the turn and reach the speed of the traffic you are joining without disrupting it.

question.text: What does mindful driving mean?

answer.text: Mindful driving means being mentally present with phone and entertainment off, prepared by scanning ahead, and proactive in adjusting to road, weather and traffic.

teaching.text: Mindful driving means present, prepared and proactive, with phone and entertainment off. Remember: present, prepared, proactive.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Mindful driving means being mentally present with phone and entertainment off, prepared by scanning ahead, and proactive in adjusting to road, weather and traffic.

question.text: How many things can your brain focus on at once, and where should your attention be?

answer.text: Your brain can focus on only one thing at a time, so line up your mental attention with where your eyes are looking.

teaching.text: Your brain focuses on one thing at a time, so keep your attention where your eyes are. Remember: attention follows your eyes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your brain can focus on only one thing at a time, so line up your mental attention with where your eyes are looking.

question.text: How long does a distraction need to last to be dangerous?

answer.text: Even a distraction lasting a few seconds can have devastating results, so remove distractions from inside and outside the car.

teaching.text: Even a few seconds of distraction can be devastating, so remove distractions. Remember: seconds can be devastating.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Even a distraction lasting a few seconds can have devastating results, so remove distractions from inside and outside the car.

question.text: What three kinds of vision do drivers use, and how does speed affect them?

answer.text: Drivers use central, fringe and peripheral vision, and higher speeds lower the quality of all of them.

teaching.text: Central, fringe and peripheral vision all get worse at higher speeds. Remember: speed dulls all vision.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Drivers use central, fringe and peripheral vision, and higher speeds lower the quality of all of them.

question.text: What does each kind of vision cover?

answer.text: Central vision shows detail straight ahead, fringe vision sees edges without sharp focus, and peripheral vision covers what is off to your side.

teaching.text: Central shows detail ahead, fringe sees soft edges, peripheral covers your sides. Remember: detail, edges, sides.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Central vision shows detail straight ahead, fringe vision sees edges without sharp focus, and peripheral vision covers what is off to your side.

question.text: How do central, fringe and peripheral vision differ?

answer.text: Central vision is for detail straight ahead, fringe vision is seen but not sharp, and peripheral vision is what lies to your sides.

teaching.text: Central is sharp, fringe is soft, peripheral is to the side. Remember: sharp, soft, side.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Central vision is for detail straight ahead, fringe vision is seen but not sharp, and peripheral vision is what lies to your sides.

question.text: What is your path of travel, and when do you change it?

answer.text: Your path of travel is the route you drive between places, and you will change it for hazards, weather or a new direction by picturing a new target area.

teaching.text: Your path of travel is your route, changed by picturing a new target area. Remember: route between places.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your path of travel is the route you drive between places, and you will change it for hazards, weather or a new direction by picturing a new target area.

question.text: What is line of sight?

answer.text: Line of sight is everything between you and the target area you picked, and you switch attention between it and your path of travel quickly and often.

teaching.text: Line of sight is everything between you and your chosen target area. Remember: you to the target.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Line of sight is everything between you and the target area you picked, and you switch attention between it and your path of travel quickly and often.

question.text: How does path of travel differ from line of sight?

answer.text: Path of travel is the route you drive, while line of sight is only the stretch between you and the target area you chose on that route.

teaching.text: Path of travel is the route; line of sight is your view to the target. Remember: route versus view.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Path of travel is the route you drive, while line of sight is only the stretch between you and the target area you chose on that route.

question.text: Among what must your attention be shared?

answer.text: Your attention must be shared among your path, line of sight, target area, hazards, your vehicle inside and out, other road users and yourself.

teaching.text: Share attention among your path, target, hazards, vehicle, other users and yourself. Remember: share attention widely.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your attention must be shared among your path, line of sight, target area, hazards, your vehicle inside and out, other road users and yourself.

question.text: At night, how slowly should you drive, and how far do headlights usually reach?

answer.text: At night, drive slowly enough to stop within the reach of your headlights, which is usually four hundred feet.

teaching.text: At night, drive slowly enough to stop within your headlights, usually four hundred feet. Remember: stop within your lights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night, drive slowly enough to stop within the reach of your headlights, which is usually four hundred feet.

question.text: When should you use high beams?

answer.text: Use high beams whenever no vehicles are coming toward you, and switch to regular headlights when traffic approaches.

teaching.text: Use high beams when no one is coming, and dim when traffic approaches. Remember: high beams when empty ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use high beams whenever no vehicles are coming toward you, and switch to regular headlights when traffic approaches.

question.text: Which headlights do you use when following another vehicle?

answer.text: Use regular headlights, not high beams, when you are following another vehicle.

teaching.text: Use regular headlights when following another vehicle. Remember: regular lights when following.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use regular headlights, not high beams, when you are following another vehicle.

question.text: When do you switch from high beams to regular headlights?

answer.text: High beams are for roads with no oncoming vehicles, and you dim to regular headlights as soon as traffic approaches.

teaching.text: High beams only with no oncoming traffic; dim as soon as it approaches. Remember: dim when traffic comes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: High beams are for roads with no oncoming vehicles, and you dim to regular headlights as soon as traffic approaches.

question.text: What do you do if an oncoming driver keeps high beams on?

answer.text: If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, look toward the right side of the road instead of into the lights.

teaching.text: Facing oncoming high beams, look toward the right side of the road. Remember: look right, not at glare.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, look toward the right side of the road instead of into the lights.

question.text: Facing oncoming high beams, where do you look?

answer.text: Facing an oncoming driver with high beams on, you shift your eyes toward the right side of the road rather than looking into the glare.

teaching.text: Look toward the right side, not into oncoming glare. Remember: eyes to the right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Facing an oncoming driver with high beams on, you shift your eyes toward the right side of the road rather than looking into the glare.

question.text: How should you scan at night?

answer.text: At night, look past your headlight beams for dark shapes and glance to the sides to find the pavement edge and side hazards.

teaching.text: At night, look past your beams for dark shapes and glance to the sides. Remember: look past your beams.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night, look past your headlight beams for dark shapes and glance to the sides to find the pavement edge and side hazards.

question.text: When should you not wear sunglasses or colored lenses?

answer.text: Do not wear sunglasses or colored lenses at night or on overcast days, because tinted lenses cut your vision.

teaching.text: Skip sunglasses and tinted lenses at night and on overcast days. Remember: no tint at night.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not wear sunglasses or colored lenses at night or on overcast days, because tinted lenses cut your vision.

question.text: How should following distance change at night?

answer.text: Lengthen your following distance at night, and especially on unfamiliar roads after dark.

teaching.text: Lengthen your following distance at night, especially on unfamiliar roads. Remember: more distance after dark.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Lengthen your following distance at night, and especially on unfamiliar roads after dark.

question.text: When should you slow down to keep control?

answer.text: Slow down before a sharp curve, on slippery pavement, or when water is on the road so you keep control of the vehicle.

teaching.text: Slow down before sharp curves, on slippery pavement and when water is on the road. Remember: slow for curves, water.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow down before a sharp curve, on slippery pavement, or when water is on the road so you keep control of the vehicle.

question.text: When should you slow down for a curve?

answer.text: Reduce speed before you enter a curve, not in it, to keep traction; uphill curves may need more gas and downhill curves more braking.

teaching.text: Slow before the curve, not in it, to keep traction. Remember: slow before the curve.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Reduce speed before you enter a curve, not in it, to keep traction; uphill curves may need more gas and downhill curves more braking.

question.text: Where in your lane should you approach a curve?

answer.text: Approach a curve positioned slightly toward the outside of your lane for more room and a better view around it.

teaching.text: Approach a curve slightly toward the outside of your lane. Remember: slightly toward the outside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Approach a curve positioned slightly toward the outside of your lane for more room and a better view around it.

question.text: How do you drive inside a curve?

answer.text: Inside a curve, hold a steady speed and steer gently, avoiding sudden braking, sudden acceleration or jerky steering that can upset balance.

teaching.text: Inside a curve, hold a steady speed and steer gently. Remember: steady and gentle.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Inside a curve, hold a steady speed and steer gently, avoiding sudden braking, sudden acceleration or jerky steering that can upset balance.

question.text: How do you leave a curve?

answer.text: Leaving a curve, speed up gradually and check your mirrors before merging or changing lanes.

teaching.text: Leaving a curve, speed up gradually and check mirrors before changing lanes. Remember: build speed gradually.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Leaving a curve, speed up gradually and check your mirrors before merging or changing lanes.

question.text: How does your speed change before, inside and after a curve?

answer.text: Speed comes off before the curve, stays steady inside it, and builds back gradually on the way out.

teaching.text: Slow before the curve, steady inside, build speed after. Remember: slow, steady, build.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Speed comes off before the curve, stays steady inside it, and builds back gradually on the way out.

question.text: What are roll and yaw?

answer.text: Roll is how much the vehicle tilts in a turn and yaw is its side-to-side movement, and adjusting speed and steering balances both in curves.

teaching.text: Roll is the tilt in a turn and yaw is side-to-side movement. Remember: tilt and sway.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Roll is how much the vehicle tilts in a turn and yaw is its side-to-side movement, and adjusting speed and steering balances both in curves.

question.text: What does inertia do in a curve?

answer.text: Inertia tries to keep the car going straight, so a sudden turn of the wheel in a curve works against you and steering must be smooth.

teaching.text: Inertia keeps the car going straight, so steer smoothly in curves. Remember: inertia wants straight.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Inertia tries to keep the car going straight, so a sudden turn of the wheel in a curve works against you and steering must be smooth.

question.text: How does speed relate to kinetic energy?

answer.text: More speed means more kinetic energy and more time and space needed to stop or turn, so slowing for curves helps you keep traction.

teaching.text: More speed means more kinetic energy and more room needed to stop or turn. Remember: more speed, more energy.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: More speed means more kinetic energy and more time and space needed to stop or turn, so slowing for curves helps you keep traction.

question.text: What gives your tires grip, and what reduces it?

answer.text: Friction between tires and road is what lets you grip, and rain, snow or ice can sharply reduce it in curves, so slow down even more there.

teaching.text: Friction is your grip, and rain, snow or ice can sharply reduce it. Remember: friction is your grip.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Friction between tires and road is what lets you grip, and rain, snow or ice can sharply reduce it in curves, so slow down even more there.

question.text: What are inertia, kinetic energy and friction?

answer.text: Inertia is the pull to keep going straight, kinetic energy is what grows with speed, and friction is the grip between tires and road.

teaching.text: Inertia keeps you straight, kinetic energy grows with speed, friction grips. Remember: straight, speed, grip.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Inertia is the pull to keep going straight, kinetic energy is what grows with speed, and friction is the grip between tires and road.

question.text: How must you drive on slippery roads?

answer.text: On slippery roads you must adjust to conditions, which can mean driving below the posted limit.

teaching.text: Slippery roads may require driving below the posted limit. Remember: below limit if slippery.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On slippery roads you must adjust to conditions, which can mean driving below the posted limit.

question.text: Why is the road very slippery when rain begins on a hot day?

answer.text: When rain begins on a hot day, the road is very slippery for the first few minutes because heat brings oil in the asphalt to the surface until it washes off.

teaching.text: On a hot day, the first minutes of rain are very slippery from surfaced oil. Remember: first rain, oily road.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When rain begins on a hot day, the road is very slippery for the first few minutes because heat brings oil in the asphalt to the surface until it washes off.

question.text: When is the danger greatest after rain begins on a hot day?

answer.text: When rain starts on a hot day the danger is at the start, since the road stays very slippery for the first few minutes until the surfaced oil washes away.

teaching.text: On a hot day, the danger is in the first minutes of rain. Remember: danger at the start.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When rain starts on a hot day the danger is at the start, since the road stays very slippery for the first few minutes until the surfaced oil washes away.

question.text: How should you drive on snowy roads?

answer.text: Snowy roads call for a much larger following distance and a greatly reduced speed.

teaching.text: On snow, greatly reduce speed and greatly increase following distance. Remember: slow way down in snow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Snowy roads call for a much larger following distance and a greatly reduced speed.

question.text: When should you use snow tires or chains?

answer.text: Use snow tires or chains where they are required, and in winter chains or studded tires can improve traction.

teaching.text: Use snow tires or chains where required; chains or studs improve winter traction. Remember: chains where required.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use snow tires or chains where they are required, and in winter chains or studded tires can improve traction.

question.text: Where can ice form when the rest of the road is clear?

answer.text: Shady spots on cold, wet days and bridges or overpasses can be icy even when the rest of the road is not.

teaching.text: Bridges, overpasses and shady spots can be icy when the rest of the road is clear. Remember: bridges and shade ice first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Shady spots on cold, wet days and bridges or overpasses can be icy even when the rest of the road is not.

question.text: What happens as ice warms toward freezing?

answer.text: Ice warming from below freezing to near freezing gets wet on top and becomes even more slippery.

teaching.text: Ice warming toward freezing gets wet and even more slippery. Remember: wet ice is worse.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Ice warming from below freezing to near freezing gets wet on top and becomes even more slippery.

question.text: Where can ice hide, and what makes ice more slippery?

answer.text: Bridges, overpasses and shady spots can be icy while the rest of the road is clear, and ice that warms toward freezing turns wet and makes the road more slippery, not less.

teaching.text: Ice hides on bridges and in shade, and warming ice is more slippery. Remember: warming ice, hidden ice.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bridges, overpasses and shady spots can be icy while the rest of the road is clear, and ice that warms toward freezing turns wet and makes the road more slippery, not less.

question.text: What is black ice, and when should you watch for it?

answer.text: Black ice is a thin, hard-to-see coating of ice, so stay alert whenever temperatures are near or below freezing even if you see no ice.

teaching.text: Black ice is thin and hard to see, so stay alert near freezing. Remember: near freezing, think ice.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Black ice is a thin, hard-to-see coating of ice, so stay alert whenever temperatures are near or below freezing even if you see no ice.

question.text: What causes a skid, and what is the best defense?

answer.text: A skid happens when tires lose their grip, made more likely by high speed and slick roads when you turn or stop suddenly, and the best defense is avoiding one.

teaching.text: Skids come from lost grip at high speed on slick roads; avoid them first. Remember: best skid is none.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A skid happens when tires lose their grip, made more likely by high speed and slick roads when you turn or stop suddenly, and the best defense is avoiding one.

question.text: What do you do with your feet in a skid?

answer.text: In a skid, first lift your foot off the accelerator, then press or pump the brakes; without antilock brakes, stomping the pedal can worsen the skid.

teaching.text: In a skid, lift off the gas, then press or pump the brakes. Remember: off gas, then brake.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a skid, first lift your foot off the accelerator, then press or pump the brakes; without antilock brakes, stomping the pedal can worsen the skid.

question.text: How does braking in a skid differ with and without antilock brakes?

answer.text: Antilock brakes let you keep steering while braking in a skid, whereas without them a quick hard press on the pedal can deepen the skid.

teaching.text: Antilock brakes let you steer while braking; without them, hard braking deepens a skid. Remember: ABS lets you steer.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Antilock brakes let you keep steering while braking in a skid, whereas without them a quick hard press on the pedal can deepen the skid.

question.text: Which way do you steer in a skid?

answer.text: During a skid, steer the way the vehicle is moving and keep correcting until the tires regain traction in the direction you steer.

teaching.text: In a skid, steer the way the car is moving and keep correcting. Remember: steer where it's going.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: During a skid, steer the way the vehicle is moving and keep correcting until the tires regain traction in the direction you steer.

question.text: What is hydroplaning, and how do you prevent it?

answer.text: Hydroplaning is water building up between tires and road so they lose traction, and slowing down on wet roads is the best prevention.

teaching.text: Hydroplaning is water lifting the tires off the road; slow down on wet roads. Remember: slow down when wet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hydroplaning is water building up between tires and road so they lose traction, and slowing down on wet roads is the best prevention.

question.text: What do you do if you hydroplane?

answer.text: If you hydroplane, lift off the accelerator, brake gently, hold the wheel steady without jerking it, and look where you want to go.

teaching.text: If you hydroplane, ease off the gas, brake gently and hold the wheel steady. Remember: ease off, hold steady.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you hydroplane, lift off the accelerator, brake gently, hold the wheel steady without jerking it, and look where you want to go.

question.text: How does steering in a skid differ from steering while hydroplaning?

answer.text: In a skid you steer in the direction the car is moving and keep correcting, but when hydroplaning you hold the wheel steady and avoid any jerk or overcorrection.

teaching.text: Skids: steer where the car goes. Hydroplaning: hold the wheel steady. Remember: skid steers; hydroplane holds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a skid you steer in the direction the car is moving and keep correcting, but when hydroplaning you hold the wheel steady and avoid any jerk or overcorrection.

question.text: Why brake gently when hydroplaning?

answer.text: Without antilock brakes, pressing the pedal hard while hydroplaning can make it worse, which is why the guide says to brake gently.

teaching.text: Brake gently when hydroplaning, since hard braking without antilock brakes worsens it. Remember: hard braking worsens it.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Without antilock brakes, pressing the pedal hard while hydroplaning can make it worse, which is why the guide says to brake gently.

hooks_spoken: Turn into traffic only with room to match its speed, drive mentally present, and focus where you look.
Even a few seconds of distraction can be devastating.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of mindful driving. Turn into traffic only with room to match its speed, drive mentally present, and focus where you look. Even a few seconds of distraction can be devastating. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Drive slowly enough to stop within your headlights, and use high beams only with no one ahead.

recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of night driving. Drive slowly enough to stop within your headlights, and use high beams only with no one ahead. Look right for glare, look past your beams, skip tinted lenses and add following distance. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Slow before the curve, approach toward the outside, hold steady inside, and build speed on the way out.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of curves. Slow before the curve, approach toward the outside, hold steady inside, and build speed on the way out. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of forces in curves. Roll and yaw shift the car, inertia pulls straight, speed builds energy, and friction is your grip. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.
